newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Moscow eyes higher duty on aluminium raw materials.
newsitem.headline: Moscow eyes higher duty on aluminium raw materials.

text.p: Russia is considering higher trade duties on raw materials brought in by Western commodity powerhouses for refining by huge aluminium plants, according to documents obtained by Reuters on Wednesday.

In an official order signed by Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin dated July 3, the government called on the Foreign Ministry and other state bodies to consider raising trade duties on imports of raw materials used to make primary aluminium.

"The Russian government orders the Foreign Trade Ministry together with other interested federal parties to look into the possibility of increasing trade duties on imported raw materials," the order said, providing no further details.

It also proposed a single value-added tax system for both resident and non-resident firms in Russia's aluminium industry, effectively raising non-residents' costs because they pay less VAT than residents, or none at all, officials said.
It was not immediately clear when or even if the proposals would become law.
But they were almost bound to spark another row over the extent of foreign control of one of Russia's most promising industrial sectors.

Russia is the world's largest exporter of aluminium, a base metal used in applications ranging from car body parts to drink cans. It exported 2.44 million tonnes in 1996, or 85 percent of its output of 2.87 million tonnes.
But it relies heavily on international commodity powerhouses like Swiss-based Glencore AG and London-based Trans-World Group to provide it with raw materials like alumina.
Huge refining plants, the biggest of which are in Siberia, then process the materials and hand the refined product back to the trade houses to export under so-called "tolling" deals.
Tolling, a multi-billion-dollar business, accounts for around 70 percent of Russian output.

Any rise in duties on imported raw materials could seriously affect tolling and make life difficult for Western trading firms, which many in the industry feel have muscled their way into a strong position in the sector.
"Any rise in taxes will reduce non-residents' activity (in aluminium)," said Alexander Isayev of Kontsern Alyuminiy, a Moscow-based aluminium and alumina producers' group.
The proposal to consider hiking duties could also fill government coffers as Moscow searches for cash to pay off salary arrears to the public sector and keep reforms on track.
"I always felt sure the Russian government would come in with a new form of tax (on tolling)," said a senior Western aluminium trader.
"More money would go into government coffers, and they would get greater control of the aluminium industry."

Not everyone is for slamming the door on trading companies. Smelter officials say that without foreign suppliers, some plants would have ceased to operate altogether after Moscow disbanded Russia's centralised economy in 1991.
And some aluminium officials said this was still a risk.
"If the government increases duties on imported raw materials, then the financial position of our own smelters will worsen," Isayev said.
He said the government might well back down from its proposals for the aluminium industry when it saw that tolling was still crucial to the survival of many plants.
"This would be a step in the wrong direction...and I don't think the government will determine against its own industry."
But the trader said the government had a fair chance of pushing the measures through.

If trading companies' tolling activities were curtailed by a hike in duty, cash-strapped smelters would still have to rely on a third party, possibly the government, to pay for a large proportion of their raw materials.
"Whether it is the trading houses or the government, someone will have to support the smelters financially," the trader said.
Calls to curb foreign participation in Russia's aluminium industry earlier this year helped push prices to 14-month highs on the London Metal Exchange in March.
